uncited: It sets itself apart from sibling techniques like [Speedlines](link) (which use cones/lines) and [Opacity Modulation](link) (which uses transparency) by generating discrete, geometric tube-like silhouettes that represent the feature's past positions.
The method operates on a vector field and a geometric feature $f$ defined on an unstructured mesh.
It constructs a series of offset contours representing the feature's motion history.
*   Feature geometry $f$ (surface or boundary).
*   Velocity data associated with the feature (instantaneous average velocity $v_{avg}$).
*   A mesh geometry containing the original feature and a series of offset cylindrical silhouettes.
*   **Receding Curve ($s$):** A subsequence of points from $bc$ representing the receding portion.
*   **Offset Curve ($s_{new}$):** A sequence of 3D points representing the shifted silhouette.
**Receding Portion Extraction:** Reduce $bc$ to the receding portion $s$.
Calculating the distance $d_i$ for each point $p_i$ in $bc$ relative to the direction of motion (see Formula).
**Initial Offset:** Calculate the offset vector $V = v_{avg} \cdot \Delta t$.
For each point $i$ in the offset curve $s$, calculate its distance $d_i$ using Equation 11.
This ensures the silhouette starts at the rear-most edge of the feature relative to motion.
**First Silhouette Generation:** Extrude the trimmed curve $s$ into cylinders (tubes) using a built-in mesh generation filter (e.g., VTK `TubeFilter`) with parameters $r_{init}$ and $F_{facets}$.
**Generate:** Extrude the new curve $s$ into cylinders.
Reduce the tube diameter by the reduction factor $\alpha$ relative to the previous step.
*   $p_i$ is the position of point $i$ on the contour.
*   $c$ is the centroid of the feature or contour.
*   $v_{avg}$ is the average feature velocity vector.
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of points in the bounding contour and the number of strobes $N$.
The dominant costs are the contour extraction, smoothing (DCT/Gaussian), and tube generation per iteration.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Proportional to the number of points in the contour multiplied by $N$ (for the stored silhouette points) plus the mesh storage for the generated tubes.
It is computationally efficient compared to full temporal volume compositing.
It only visualizes the "receding" portion, potentially ignoring leading-edge history.
Accuracy depends heavily on the quality of the velocity field and contour extraction.
*   **When to use:** When the user needs to understand the trajectory and deformation of a specific feature boundary over a short time interval in a static view.
*   **When not to use:** When the velocity field is highly non-uniform or turbulent, or when the full volumetric history (not just the boundary) is required.
It is distinct from "Speedlines" (which use cones) and "Opacity Modulation" (which uses transparency) within the same family of techniques.
